opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is that you get to sit at an unusual intersection. At AISI, you're close enough to the technical frontier that you can actually engage with the research, run experiments, and form your own views about where things are going. But you're also inside government, so you have a channel into how those views get used: how policymakers think about risk, what questions they're asking, and what evidence they need to make decisions.

As a senior researcher, a lot of the value is in judgment and taste rather than raw output. A lot of what I do is help decide which problems are worth working on: which research directions are likely to matter if things go well, and which matter if things go badly. Then I try to help people on the team avoid the dead ends I've seen before. Having spent time at places like OpenAI and DeepMind, I've watched a fair number of research agendas play out, and some of that pattern-matching transfers.

There's also a translation role. The technical community and the policy community often talk past each other. Researchers will say something carefully hedged and it gets read as either "everything's fine" or "the sky is falling." Being able to say, "Here's what we actually know, here's what we don't, and here's how confident you should be," is surprisingly valuable, and it's hard to do well unless you're both technically credible and trusted on the government side.

And finally, there's a field-building aspect. AISI can fund and direct work beyond its own walls. For example, it can set up grant programs for alignment research or put out research agendas saying, "These are the problems we think are important and underexplored." A senior person can help shape those agendas so the broader research ecosystem moves toward the questions that matter most for safety, rather than just the ones that are easiest to publish on.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing I'd emphasise is that AISI sits in an unusual position. We're a government body, so we have a kind of access and a kind of mandate that academic labs and even the frontier companies don't have. We can go to the labs and say, "We'd like to look at your model before it ships," and they'll give us that access. And that means the research we do isn't abstract — it's pointed at the actual systems that are about to be deployed in the world.

For a senior researcher, that's quite special. In most places, you spend a lot of effort trying to figure out what the important problems are, and then a lot more effort trying to convince anyone that your results matter. Here, the problems come to you. The question of "is this model dangerous in some particular way, and how would we even know?" is sitting right there, and there's a direct line from answering it to decisions that governments and companies actually make.

The other piece is that a lot of the hard problems in evaluation and safety are genuinely open research problems, not just engineering. How do you elicit capabilities properly? How do you know when your evaluation is lying to you because the model is sandbagging? How do you build a safety case that would actually stand up to scrutiny? Those need people who can do rigorous, careful work and also tolerate a lot of mess, because the ground is shifting every few months.

And then the leverage of being senior there is that you can shape what the organisation thinks is worth doing. We're still relatively young. The research agenda isn't fixed. If you come in with a good argument for why some class of evaluations or some safety-case methodology matters, you can quite quickly find that the whole team is working on it. That's a kind of influence over the field that's hard to get elsewhere — you're not just publishing a paper and hoping someone reads it, you're setting what gets measured, and what gets measured ends up being what the labs optimise for.

So, roughly: real access, real problems, real consequences, and a lot of room to steer. That's what I find valuable about it.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the value is in helping people make good research decisions under uncertainty. At AISI, you want work that’s technically strong, but you also want it to bear on the questions that matter for AI safety. And there often isn’t a straightforward recipe for connecting those two things.

A senior researcher can help someone take a broad concern and turn it into a concrete question: What experiment would actually teach us something? If we got this result, what would we conclude? What would we still not know? That kind of guidance can save a lot of time, while still leaving people room to develop their own ideas.

And I think there’s value in being involved in the technical work yourself. Your advice is much better if you’re close enough to the research to understand where the difficulties are. So the role I find attractive is a combination of doing research and helping other people do research well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of the value is in helping people work out what the right questions are. There are lots of things you could measure about a model, and lots of experiments you could run. The harder question is: which of those would actually change our understanding of the risks, or inform a decision someone needs to make?

A senior researcher can help connect those levels: take a fairly broad concern, turn it into a concrete research question, and help a team design an experiment whose results we can interpret. And part of that is being willing to say, “This result is interesting, but it doesn’t establish the thing we were hoping to establish.”

There’s also a mentoring role. You want people to develop their own judgement, rather than have every decision run through you. If you can help a team get better at choosing problems and being clear about what the evidence does and doesn’t show, that has much more impact than just doing your own research.
